entry.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

link.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

entry.content:
Fine-tuning an open model used to mean writing a training script: dataset glue, tokenizer surgery, trainer arguments, sharding flags, and a prayer that the checkpoint resumes. Axolotl replaces the script with a single YAML file and a codebase whose whole architecture exists to translate that YAML into a correct, memory-efficient training run. The result is one of the most widely used fine-tuning frameworks in the open-source world, and its source is a masterclass in how to layer configuration, data, and distributed training without letting any of them tangle. Version 0.21.1 under an Apache-2.0 license, it currently spans roughly 750 Python modules under its src tree, covering everything from classic Alpaca prompt formats to NVFP4 MoE LoRA kernels and asynchronous GRPO rollouts.

What makes the codebase worth reading is that it is honest about the messy parts. Every performance trick you have heard about - sample packing, flash attention swaps, FSDP2 with 4-bit bases, fused Liger kernels - lives here as an actual patch or plugin with clear seams, not as a blog diagram. You can trace one YAML key from the schema that validates it, through the loader that acts on it, to the trainer mixin that consumes it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI and config layer feeds dataset machinery and model loading; the trainer core consumes packed batches while patches and plugins reshape the model in between.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli/main.py is the dispatcher whose main at line 529 wires every subcommand from train to preprocess to merge to cloud launches.
  • utils/config/init.py at 636 lines reads the YAML, applies defaults and plugin additions, and hands it to validation.
  • utils/schemas/config.py defines AxolotlInputConfig at line 196, a 2240-line pydantic schema that is effectively the framework’s contract with users.
  • utils/data/sft.py starts at prepare_datasets line 49 and assembles raw, tokenized, and shuffled datasets for supervised runs.
  • prompt_strategies/chat_template.py implements ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308, turning chat rows into masked label tensors.
  • utils/samplers/multipack.py provides MultipackBatchSampler at line 252, the best-fit-decreasing bin packer that keeps sequences together.
  • loaders/model.py is ModelLoader at line 209, 1468 lines handling quantization configs, device maps, and attention impl selection.
  • train.py closes the loop with train at line 703: setup, execute, save, model card, plugin teardown.

Why You Need This

If you have read our tours of peft, accelerate, or deepspeed, you know the individual parts: adapters, sharding, ZeRO stages. Axolotl is the orchestration layer that binds them behind one config file, and reading it shows you what integration actually costs. The repo does not just call PEFT’s get_peft_model; it patches PEFT’s parameter wrappers, seeds adapter initialization deterministically, and validates that a saved adapter matches the patterns you asked for. Those are the failure modes you only discover after your third night-long run dies at step 4000.

It is also the best available map of the 2025-2026 fine-tuning frontier in executable form. QLoRA on FSDP2 without a full-precision replica per GPU, NVFP4 MoE adapters via custom Triton kernels, selective activation checkpointing with CPU offload, asynchronous GRPO with a rollout producer - each landed as a self-contained module you can read in isolation. When a technique confuses you in a paper, the odds are good this repo contains the production version of it. Our torchtitan tour showed a clean-room trainer; axolotl shows the same ideas bolted onto the Hugging Face ecosystem where most practitioners actually live.

Finally, the plugin architecture is a lesson in extension design. Liger kernels, the ScatterMoE LoRA library, evaluation hooks, and even cloud launchers all enter through the same BasePlugin contract, getting called at pre-config-load, pre-model-load, post-model-load, and post-train phases. Nothing core knows Liger exists; the patch manager just asks registered plugins to do their worst at defined moments. If you maintain any training tool and want to stop merging every user request into core, this is the pattern to steal.

Detailed view: entry and config, dataset machinery, model and adapter loading, the trainer core, RL and preference trainers, and the patch and kernel layer.

Start at the entry, because the config is the product. cli/train.py defines do_cli at line 88 and do_train at line 37; the config path lands in utils/config/init.py which merges plugin-added keys before utils/schemas/config.py validates against AxolotlInputConfig at line 196. The schema is worth an evening: every knob from sequence_len to flash_attention is declared with types and defaults, and a capability-aware subclass AxolotlConfigWCapabilities at line 1939 cross-references the declared attention implementation against the installed hardware before a single GPU is touched. When validation fails you get a pydantic error pointing at the exact key, not a CUDA OOM nine hours later.

The dataset machinery is the second act. utils/data/sft.py loads raw datasets at line 319, applies the selected strategy through prompt_strategies/chat_template.py whose ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308 builds input and label tensors from any Jinja chat template, and persists the tokenized result so runs after the first skip straight to loading at line 268. The strategy ABCs live in prompt_tokenizers.py with PromptTokenizingStrategy at line 43, and the legacy Alpaca family at line 162 shows how train-on-input masking works. For RL runs the parallel module utils/data/rl.py at 528 lines prepares preference and prompt datasets instead.

The packing story is where axolotl earns its throughput. utils/samplers/multipack.py implements MultipackBatchSampler at line 252: sequence lengths come in, ffd_check at line 33 validates the bin estimate, pack_group at line 69 does best-fit-decreasing, and generate_batches at line 378 emits index batches whose padding waste is reported by efficiency at line 597. The sampler plugs into AxolotlTrainer through _create_multipack_sampler at line 363 of core/trainers/base.py, and the matching collator V2BatchSamplerDataCollatorForSeq2Seq at line 213 of utils/collators/batching.py pads to the batch max rather than a global max. A monkeypatch teaches the stock HF Trainer about these variable-length batches so loss normalization counts real tokens, a detail that silently skews results if ignored.

Model loading is a 1468-line negotiation with reality. ModelLoader.load at line 313 of loaders/model.py runs pre-model-load patches, picks device map via _set_device_map_config at line 922, quantization via _set_quantization_config at line 1006, and attention via _set_attention_config at line 1105, then _build_model at line 1243 actually constructs the model and _build_adapters at line 727 attaches LoRA through loaders/adapter.py whose load_lora at line 414 and find_all_linear_names at line 60 decide what gets adapters. The deepest magic is monkeypatch/accelerate/fsdp2.py: fsdp2_load_full_state_dict at line 183 shards a full checkpoint across ranks while keeping 4-bit quantized parameters intact, fsdp2_prepare_model at line 583 applies activation checkpointing, and the QLoRA companion monkeypatch/fsdp2_qlora.py makes adapters trainable on the sharded quantized base - the CPU-staged loading that lets you fine-tune models bigger than any single GPU.

On top sit the trainers and plugins. AxolotlTrainer at line 114 of core/trainers/base.py overrides compute_loss at line 771 for proper token-level normalization and composes mixins from core/trainers/mixins/packing.py. RL lives in core/trainers/grpo/trainer.py with AxolotlGRPOTrainer at line 57 and a context-parallel variant at line 89 whose _generate_and_score_completions at line 297 does the rollout-scoring dance, while core/trainers/grpo/async_trainer.py builds a full producer-consumer system - AsyncDataProducer at line 368, RolloutDataset at line 529, AsyncGRPOTrainer at line 832 - so generation overlaps training. Plugins enter through integrations/base.py; LigerPlugin at line 34 of integrations/liger/plugin.py swaps fused kernels in pre_model_load at line 114, and KernelsPlugin at line 146 of integrations/kernels/plugin.py routes MoE adapters to the ScatterMoE library’s grouped kernels while registering house Triton ops like the swiglu in kernels/swiglu.py.

What happens after the last step matters just as much, and the post-training exit ramps are built in. train at line 703 of train.py finishes with save_trained_model at line 274, which handles the FSDP merge-and-rename path (a helper at line 252 renames merged shards to adapter form), writes the model card at line 488, and calls PluginManager.post_train so plugins can unload or upload. From there the CLI takes over: cli/merge_lora.py collapses adapters into base weights with a memory-efficient variant at line 119, and the export command drives utils/gguf.py whose export_gguf at line 149 resolves llama.cpp binaries, preflights the vocab and template at line 89, and quantizes straight to a deployable GGUF for llama.cpp or Ollama. A fine-tune that ends in a serving-ready file without leaving the tool is the actual deliverable most users want.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s uv-first install and one-command train:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export UV_TORCH_BACKEND=cu130
uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install torch==2.14.0 torchvision
uv pip install --no-build-isolation axolotl[deepspeed]
axolotl fetch examples
axolotl train examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml

The same path programmatically, which is how notebooks and sweeps drive it:

from axolotl.cli.train import do_cli

do_cli(config="examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml")

Change a few keys - base_model, learning_rate, lora_target_modules, flash_attention: true - and the identical command fine-tunes a different architecture; add rl: grpo with a reward function and the same entrypoint switches to the GRPO trainer.

Honest limits: axolotl’s breadth is also its surface area - the monkeypatch and model_support trees track upstream Hugging Face and torch releases closely, so pinning versions matters more here than in smaller tools. The config schema documents most keys, but exotic combinations (NVFP4 MoE plus context parallelism, say) carry caveats that only the docs’ support matrix admits to. And like every YAML-driven trainer, it will happily train a mediocre model on a mediocre dataset; no framework validates that your data was worth the GPU hours.
entry.summary: A source tour of axolotl, the configuration-driven fine-tuning framework: pydantic config validation, prompt strategies, multipack bin-packing, FSDP2 QLoRA patches, plugin integrations, and GRPO trainers.

entry.title: 100+ Models, One Command - Inside hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory
entry.content:
Where axolotl bets on one exhaustive YAML schema, LLaMA-Factory bets on breadth: one CLI that fine-tunes over a hundred model families, one data loader that speaks every open dataset format, and one stage dispatcher that walks from continuous pretraining through supervised fine-tuning into reward modeling, PPO, DPO, and KTO. The project behind the widely cited “Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models” paper has become the default answer to “how do I fine-tune X” for a whole generation of practitioners, and it ships a Gradio web UI so the entire journey runs from a browser. Apache-2.0 licensed, it packs its power into a surprisingly compact src tree of about 180 Python files - most of the surface area lives in a handful of genuinely enormous modules.

Those big modules are the story. A 2686-line template file encodes every supported chat format as data; a 3502-line multimodal plugin file teaches every vision-language family how to emit training rows; a 978-line trainer utilities file carries the callbacks and metrics every stage shares. Reading the repo is really reading three or four epic files plus a lattice of small workflow scripts that glue them together. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI routes to a stage dispatcher; argument parsing, the template registry, and dataset processing feed model loading and the workflows; a chat facade serves the result.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli.py is a 31-line console entry that forwards every subcommand to the launcher.
  • launcher.py at 185 lines routes train, chat, api, export, webui, and eval to their implementations.
  • hparams/parser.py defines get_train_args at line 395, fusing five argument families into one validated tuple.
  • train/tuner.py exposes run_exp at line 163 with the stage dispatch at line 69.
  • data/loader.py loads and merges datasets via get_dataset at line 276 with caching at line 229.
  • data/template.py is the template registry: register_template at line 681 defines every supported chat format.
  • data/processor/supervised.py tokenizes rows in SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51.
  • model/loader.py builds the model while chat/chat_model.py serves it afterwards.

Why You Need This

Every fine-tuning tool solves the same four problems - arguments, data, model prep, training loop - and comparing implementations is the fastest way to understand the trade space. Where the axolotl tour showed a pydantic schema validating one giant YAML, LLaMA-Factory shows the Hugging Face idiom: five dataclass families (model, data, training, finetuning, generating) parsed from CLI or dict and cross-verified in _verify_model_args at line 227 of the parser. Neither is wrong; seeing both teaches you what a config system must guarantee regardless of style. The same comparison holds for adapters - this repo’s model/adapter.py implements full, freeze, and LoRA tuning side by side, next to the PEFT internals we covered in the peft tour.

The template registry deserves particular attention because it quietly carries the entire “100+ models” claim. A chat model fine-tune is useless if the prompt format does not match the pretrained format, and this file turns that compatibility problem into data: each register_template call declares system messages, user and assistant wrappers, stop tokens, and tool-call encodings for one family. New model support lands as a few lines of registration rather than a fork of the trainer - which is exactly why the README’s day-0 support table keeps filling in. If you maintain any chat-adjacent system, this is the most complete public catalog of what varies between chat formats.

Multimodal support is the other eye-opener. The data/mm_plugin.py file gives every vision-language family - LLaVA, Gemma 3, InternVL, Kimi-VL and more - a plugin that converts raw rows into the exact interleave of text and image/video tokens that family’s model class expects, including pixel-value preprocessing and image token splicing. Rather than one generic VLM loader, the repo embraces per-family reality. And when the current architecture finally hits its limits, the v1 subtree shows the rewrite: a cleaner engine split (data_engine, model_engine, base_trainer) with its own plugin system - worth reading as a case study in how projects migrate themselves.

Detailed view: entry and dispatch, argument families, the data machinery with templates and multimodal plugins, model preparation, the six stage trainers, and the inference surface.

Follow one stage end to end. llamafactory-cli train lands in launcher.py, which calls run_exp at line 163 of train/tuner.py; read_args at line 112 of hparams/parser.py accepts either a dict or command-line tokens, and get_train_args at line 395 returns the five-class tuple after _verify_model_args at line 227 rejects contradictions like a missing template. The _training_function at line 69 then dispatches: stage sft goes to run_sft at line 41 of train/sft/workflow.py, while pt, rm, ppo, dpo, and kto each have a sibling workflow - and lines 92 through 136 show optional detours into hyper-parallel, Megatron-Bridge, and Megatron-core backends when those packages are installed.

The data path inside run_sft is the loader at work. data/loader.py merges every named dataset at line 164, converts rows via data/converter.py (alpaca, sharegpt, openai formats), resolves the chat template through get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819 of data/template.py, and hands rows to the processors: SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51 of data/processor/supervised.py builds input_ids with labels masked outside responses, its packed subclass at line 146 concatenates sequences with position-id resets, and the PairwiseDatasetProcessor at line 30 of data/processor/pairwise.py produces the chosen/rejected pairs that DPO and reward stages consume. Collators from data/collator.py finish the batches.

Model preparation is the patcher’s show. model/loader.py picks quantization through model/model_utils/quantization.py - AQLM, AWQ, GPTQ, HQQ, EETQ, and bitsandbytes variants - then model/patcher.py applies patch_config at line 365 (rope scaling, attention impl, flash-attn selection), patch_model at line 437 (longlora shift attention, packed attention, MoE and vision fixes), and unsloth support from model/model_utils/unsloth.py when requested. init_adapter at line 317 of model/adapter.py then branches: full tuning at line 38, freeze tuning at line 57, and _setup_lora_tuning at line 147 covering LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, and LoftQ variants. The workflow finishes by instantiating CustomSeq2SeqTrainer at line 47 of train/sft/trainer.py with metrics from train/trainer_utils.py.

The serving half closes the loop. ChatModel at line 39 of chat/chat_model.py wraps three engines - hf, vLLM (VllmEngine at line 46 of chat/vllm_engine.py), and sglang - behind one astream_chat interface; api/app.py exposes it as an OpenAI-compatible server; and the LLaMA Board web UI’s webui/runner.py submits training jobs straight into the same run_exp entry, so GUI and CLI are one system. Evaluation through eval/evaluator.py scores MMLU-style benchmarks with the same template machinery.

Two registries make the 100-model claim hold up. The template registry in data/template.py is a plain dict called TEMPLATES at line 678, filled by register_template at line 681 and consulted by get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819; the base Template class at line 41 carries specializations like Llama2Template at line 454 for the older Llama chat format, and ReasoningTemplate at line 524 with its Qwen38ReasoningTemplate subclass at line 593 for models that emit thinking traces before answers. Multimodal support follows the same shape in mm_plugin.py, a 3,502-line module whose BasePlugin at line 421 defines the default vision interface and whose per-family subclasses - Gemma3Plugin at line 876, InternVLPlugin at line 1180, KimiVLPlugin at line 1330, and LlavaPlugin at line 1429 - override how images and videos expand into placeholder tokens, how processor outputs are cached, and how the collator stitches visual features into the sequence. Adding a new model family usually means registering one template and one plugin instead of touching the trainer at all.

The alignment stages get their own trainers with minimal duplication. CustomDPOTrainer at line 44 of train/dpo/trainer.py extends the TRL DPOTrainer and overrides concatenated_forward at line 219 to route preference batches through the repo’s own collators and mm plugin, while CustomPPOTrainer at line 64 of train/ppo/trainer.py inherits from both PPOTrainer and Trainer to blend rollout generation with the standard optimization step. Cross-cutting behavior lands in callbacks rather than trainer edits: LogCallback at line 174 of train/callbacks.py appends each stage’s timing and loss to the trainer_log.jsonl you find in every output directory, PissaConvertCallback at line 132 swaps PiSSA adapters between their init and training representations, ReporterCallback at line 433 writes the training report when a run ends, and ModuleProfilerCallback at line 491 measures per-module memory so you can spot which layers are worth offloading or quantizing. When one node is not enough, run_exp checks ray_args.use_ray and re-enters itself through Ray, with the placement-group helpers in trainer_utils.py - get_placement_group, get_ray_head_node_ip, sort_placement_group_by_node_ip - pinning workers across the cluster, so the same YAML scales from a single GPU to a multi-node job without edits.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s zero-code loop:

uv run llamafactory-cli webui
llamafactory-cli train examples/train_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli chat examples/inference/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli export examples/merge_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml

Or programmatically, one dict instead of YAML:

from llamafactory.train.tuner import run_exp

run_exp(args={
    "stage": "sft",
    "model_name_or_path": "Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    "template": "qwen3",
    "dataset": "alpaca_en_demo",
    "finetuning_type": "lora",
    "output_dir": "qwen3-lora-out",
})

Swap stage to dpo with a pairwise dataset and the same entry runs preference tuning; point infer_backend at vllm and the same chat model serves hundreds of concurrent requests.

Honest limits: the breadth comes with weight - the giant template, mm_plugin, and trainer_utils files are dense and occasionally duplicate logic across stage trainers, so tracing one behavior can mean reading three files. The WebUI covers the happy path well but exotic combinations still want the CLI. And because so much support is template registration plus small patches, per-model quirks sometimes surface only in that model’s issue tracker, not the docs.
entry.summary: A source tour of LLaMA-Factory, the unified fine-tuning factory: a 2686-line chat template registry, multimodal plugins, stage dispatch from pretraining to PPO, and a v1 engine rewrite.

entry.title: The Ruler Every LLM Paper Trusts - Inside EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness

link.title: The Ruler Every LLM Paper Trusts - Inside EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness

entry.content:
Every benchmark number you have seen attached to an open model - MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, ARC, TruthfulQA - has a decent chance of having been produced by this repository. EleutherAI’s Language Model Evaluation Harness is the framework behind the Open LLM Leaderboard and hundreds of papers, and its power comes from an architecture that treats evaluation as data: every task is a YAML file describing prompts, document formats, and metrics, and the framework’s job is to turn any language model into a scoring function against those files. Release 0.4.14 under the MIT license ships with 221 task directories under lm_eval/tasks, each holding configs that expand into hundreds of benchmark subtasks and variants.

What makes the source worth reading is that it is a masterclass in interface design under constraint. The whole system communicates through two verbs - loglikelihood and generate_until - so anything that can answer those two requests becomes an evaluable model, from a Hugging Face checkpoint to a vLLM engine to a commercial API to a llama.cpp GGUF file. Around that spine sits a task system powerful enough to encode fewshot selection, answer extraction, and metric aggregation as declarative config, plus a plugin registry that keeps 30 model backends from tangling the core. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI drives the evaluator, which pulls tasks from the manager and requests from the model abstraction; answers flow through filters into aggregation and result logging.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • lm_eval/_cli/run.py is the 518-line entry that parses CLI flags into a simple_evaluate call.
  • lm_eval/evaluator.py holds the two public functions: simple_evaluate at line 55 and the core evaluate loop at line 429 of its 714 lines.
  • lm_eval/tasks/manager.py defines TaskManager at line 37, the indexer that turns task names into config-loaded classes.
  • lm_eval/api/task.py is the 1808-line heart: Task at line 64, ConfigurableTask at line 618.
  • lm_eval/api/model.py declares the LM interface at line 25 with TemplateLM at line 356 and CachingLM at line 275.
  • lm_eval/models/huggingface.py is the reference backend, HFLM at line 62 of 1782 lines.
  • lm_eval/api/filter.py pairs the Filter contract at line 8 with FilterEnsemble at line 34, fed by regex extractors in filters/extraction.py.
  • lm_eval/loggers/evaluation_tracker.py persists everything through EvaluationTracker at line 123.

Why You Need This

If you have followed the fine-tuning tours here - LLaMA-Factory, axolotl, unsloth - you have watched the training side of the loop. The harness is the other half: the tool that tells you whether a model got better. Reading it teaches you what benchmark numbers actually measure, because every step that could silently change a score is explicit: which prompt template was used, how many fewshot examples were sampled and by what rule, how the raw generation was cut down to an answer, and which aggregation produced the table cell. Reproducibility is not a slogan here; it is enforced by config files checked into the repo.

The backend abstraction is the lesson most applicable elsewhere. Anything implementing loglikelihood and generate_until plugs in - and the catalog shows the range: HFLM for transformers checkpoints with quantization support, VLLM for batched inference throughput, TemplateAPI for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Megatron for very large models, plus GGUF, ONNX, and Neuron variants. The same interface idea powers ctranslate2 and onnxruntime in serving, and seeing it applied to evaluation makes a strong argument for tiny, honest interfaces over framework lock-in.

The task system deserves study if you ever design datasets or leaderboards. ConfigurableTask turns a YAML file into prompt construction, target extraction, and metric selection, while the filter ensemble composes regex extraction, whitespace trimming, and majority-vote selection into the answer stage. The metric library covers everything from exact match and F1 to BLEU, chrF, perplexity, and bits-per-byte, with aggregation declared per task so nothing is hard-coded. Once you have seen how much behavior fits in declarative config, you will never hard-code an eval script again.

Detailed view: CLI entry, the evaluation core, the task API with metrics and samplers, the backend family registered against the LM interface, task definition loading, filters, and logging with caching.

The main flow starts at simple_evaluate at line 55 of evaluator.py, which resolves the model through get_model at line 613 of api/registry.py, builds the task list through a TaskManager constructed in tasks/manager.py, applies decontamination and limits, and then hands everything to evaluate at line 429 - the loop that batches requests per task, sorts them across tasks for throughput, calls the model, and routes outputs through filters and aggregation. The supporting math lands in evaluator_utils.py: get_sample_size at line 49, the aggregation accumulator at line 99, group-aware rollups through aggregate_groups at line 301, and result shaping in _process_results at line 375 of its 540 lines.

The registry is the hinge of the whole design. Registry at line 270 of api/registry.py is a generic plugin container fed by load_plugins at line 189 and import_plugins at line 246; register_model at line 587 lets any backend class join the catalog by name, DEFAULT_METRIC_REGISTRY at line 571 maps task output types to default metrics, and get_model at line 613 is the single factory call the evaluator makes. This is why the models directory can hold thirty backends - anthropic, openai_completions, textsynth, sglang, trtllm, neuron, watsonx - without the core importing any of them.

The breadth of that directory repays a skim. HFMultimodalLM at line 30 of models/hf_vlms.py extends HFLM across its 750 lines for vision-language checkpoints; MambaLMWrapper at line 10 of models/mamba_lm.py shows a state-space model joining the club through the same base class in just 164 lines; GGUFLM at line 24 of models/gguf.py implements the LM interface directly to talk to llama.cpp; and TRTLLM at line 37 of models/trtllm_causallms.py covers TensorRT-LLM deployments in 631 lines. Even audio generation gets a slot through hf_audiolm.py, and the thinness of the smaller wrappers is the point - the easier a backend is to write, the better the interface is doing its job.

Every backend implements the same small interface from api/model.py: LM at line 25 declares loglikelihood, loglikelihood_rolling, and generate_until; TemplateLM at line 356 implements the shared tokenization glue for models that expose token access; CachingLM at line 275 wraps any backend with a sqlite cache keyed by hash_args at line 255, so repeated runs replay identical requests for free. The reference implementation, HFLM at line 62 of models/huggingface.py, handles device placement, batching, PEFT adapters, and quantized checkpoints across its 1782 lines; VLLM at line 59 of models/vllm_causallms.py swaps throughput into the same contract; and TemplateAPI at line 105 of models/api_models.py does the same for remote endpoints, with shared helpers like handle_stop_sequences at line 641 of models/utils.py keeping behavior aligned.

The task layer is where YAML becomes evaluation. TaskManager at line 37 indexes every task config, tasks/_yaml_loader.py loads them with include-resolution and safe function imports through load_yaml at line 164, and tasks/_factory.py builds concrete tasks through TaskFactory at line 25. The resulting ConfigurableTask at line 618 of api/task.py is an engine of over a thousand lines that constructs fewshot contexts through ContextSampler at line 17 of api/samplers.py (with FirstNSampler, BalancedSampler at line 117, and ManualSampler variants), builds Instance requests from api/instance.py, scores outputs with the metric functions in api/metrics.py - mean at line 35, perplexity at line 47, f1_score at line 62, bleu at line 102 - and specializes into MultipleChoiceTask at line 1688 and PerplexityTask at line 1735 for the two classic evaluation shapes. Groups compose tasks hierarchically through Group at line 34 of api/group.py and ConfigurableGroup at line 346.

Answer extraction gets its own layer because raw generations rarely match gold strings directly. Filter at line 8 of api/filter.py is the contract and FilterEnsemble at line 34 chains several; filters/extraction.py provides RegexFilter at line 16, a POS-aware filter at line 66, WhitespaceFilter at line 110, and MultiChoiceRegexFilter at line 123 for multiple-choice formats, while filters/selection.py implements majority voting over sampled generations. Results finally flow through the logging stack: GeneralConfigTracker at line 38 and EvaluationTracker at line 123 of loggers/evaluation_tracker.py write samples, configs, and tables to disk or the Hub, loggers/wandb_logger.py streams the same to experiment dashboards, and the 88 lines of caching/cache.py back the request cache that makes reruns nearly instant. Even discovery is a first-class feature - lm_eval/_cli/ls.py powers lm-eval ls tasks and ls models against the same index the runner consumes.

From Install to a Benchmark Table

Install with the backends you need, then evaluate:

pip install "lm_eval[hf,vllm]"
lm_eval --model hf \
    --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b \
    --tasks hellaswag,arc_easy \
    --device cuda:0 --batch_size 8

The same run from Python:

import lm_eval

results = lm_eval.simple_evaluate(
    model="hf",
    model_args="pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b",
    tasks=["hellaswag", "arc_easy"],
    num_fewshot=0,
)
print(results["results"])

Both paths return per-task metric tables plus samples you can inspect, and the tracker writes them to JSON for later comparison.

Honest limits: benchmark scores are proxies, and the harness makes prompt and extraction choices visible but cannot make them neutral; a few backend integrations lag the latest upstream releases; and running 221 task groups naively costs real money and compute, so sane usage starts with limit and a hand-picked task list. The value of the source is that none of these limits are hidden - every choice is a line you can read.
entry.summary: A source tour of the EleutherAI evaluation harness: one YAML-driven ConfigurableTask format, a plugin registry of model backends from Hugging Face to vLLM to llama.cpp, fewshot samplers, regex answer filters, and the aggregation machinery behind benchmark tables.

entry.title: Five Calls from Data to Fine-Tuned Model - Inside OptimalScale/LMFlow

link.title: Five Calls from Data to Fine-Tuned Model - Inside OptimalScale/LMFlow

entry.content:
Every fine-tuning toolbox has a philosophy. axolotl bets on YAML, LLaMA-Factory on a hundred CLI flags, unsloth on monkey-patching, and ms-swift on mixin-composed trainers. LMFlow, from the Statistics and Machine Learning Research Group at HKUST, bets on something subtler: a small set of stable abstractions - model, dataset, and a family of aligner and tuner objects - with everything else pushed to the edges. The result is Apache-2.0 licensed, version 1.1.0, and notable for shipping its own research: RAFT (Reward rAnked FineTuning) and LISA (Layerwise Importance Sampling) were born here, the latter letting a 7B model train in 24GB without offloading. A major rewrite in July 2025 moved the stack onto Accelerate with optional extras for vLLM, SGLang, and TRL, and the project took the Best Demo Paper Award at NAACL 2024 along the way.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: examples and dataclass arguments on the left, the dataset and conversation-template layer, the model abstraction, the tuner-aligner-inferencer stages, and the optimizer and protocol libraries underneath.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • examples/finetune.py is the whole driver story in 60 lines: main at line 32 parses three argument dataclasses, requests a Finetuner from the package’s stage dispatcher, wraps a Dataset, loads a model through AutoModel, and calls tune at line 56.
  • lmflow/args.py is the 1418-line argument universe: OptimizerNames at line 34, ModelArguments at 58, DatasetArguments at 418, FinetunerArguments at 626, InferencerArguments at 853, and AutoArguments at 1408, which maps a stage name to its argument class.
  • lmflow/datasets/dataset.py defines Dataset at line 53, a backend-wrapping container with from_dict at 150, map at 309, sample at 397, train_test_split at 427, and sanity_check at 483.
  • lmflow/models/auto_model.py is a 22-line dispatch: AutoModel at line 10 routes arch_type “decoder_only” to HFDecoderModel and “text_regression” to HFTextRegressionModel.
  • lmflow/models/hf_model_mixin.py holds HFModelMixin at line 43, 608 lines of private preparation - __prepare_quant_config at 203, __prepare_peft_config at 248, __prepare_model_for_training at 323, activate_model_for_inference at 518.
  • lmflow/models/hf_decoder_model.py defines HFDecoderModel at line 57 with tokenize at 81, inference at 313, dedicated __vllm_inference at 430 and __sglang_inference at 456 branches, and merge_lora_weights at 577.
  • lmflow/optim/utils.py provides create_customized_optimizer at line 10, which synthesizes a trainer subclass whose get_optimizer_cls_and_kwargs at line 13 selects from a 22-module optimizer zoo including Muon at line 41 of muon.py and SophiaG at line 7 of sophia.py.
  • lmflow/utils/protocol.py defines DataProto at line 257, a 1067-line tensor-container module with union at 688, make_iterator at 707, and chunk at 762 - the currency for handing generation results into the next alignment round.

Why You Need This

The layering is the draw. LMFlow’s BaseModel at line 5 of lmflow/models/base_model.py is six lines long, and the HF-specific implementation arrives as a mixin you compose rather than a hierarchy you inherit: HFDecoderModel at line 57 of hf_decoder_model.py combines DecoderModel, HFModelMixin, and a six-line Tunable interface from lmflow/models/interfaces/tunable.py. If you have read trl’s trainer-centric design or ms-swift’s factory-composed trainers, this is a third point in the design space - closer to a library than a framework, which is exactly why its aligners are so easy to read.

The alignment catalog is the second reason. DPO, DPOv2, iterative DPO, RAFT, and reward-model tuning each live in their own stage class, and LMFlow does not pretend one trainer fits all: the RAFT aligner carries its own vendored 3786-line Trainer copy (RaftTrainer at line 209 of raft_trainer.py) because the algorithm predates transformers 4.35, while DPOv2 rides TRL’s DPOTrainer with a custom dpo_loss at line 102 of dpov2_trainer.py and a reward-length-penalty pairing scheme. Iterative DPO loops target-model sampling, reward scoring, and preference-pair construction in a single align method. Compare this with OpenRLHF’s single-controller PPO or axolotl’s GRPO trainers, and the algorithm-as-a-class style becomes very legible - each aligner’s align() is a readable script for one research idea.

Third, the edges of the package are full of genuinely useful tools you rarely see in one place: LISA’s DynamicLayerActivationCallback at line 8 of lisa_trainer.py is 66 lines that freeze and unfreeze layer ranges on a schedule; the optimizer zoo ships 22 implementations from AdaBelief to LARS to Muon with a README benchmark table; the Evaluator at line 46 of evaluator.py implements accuracy and perplexity paths over Accelerate and DeepSpeed; and the inferencer family includes speculative decoding (SpeculativeInferencer at line 318) and a tool-calling variant whose code_exec at line 628 runs model-emitted Python. For benchmarking the trained result, the README itself points to lm-evaluation-harness, which we toured earlier, and for LoRA internals you can pair this tour with peft and unsloth.

Detailed view: the entry dispatcher with extras-conditional registration, data and template machinery, the model abstraction, tuning with LISA, the alignment algorithm family with its vendored trainer, inference backends, and the optimizer zoo.

A run begins in examples/finetune.py: main at line 32 resolves the stage-specific argument class through AutoArguments at line 1408 of lmflow/args.py, then lets HfArgumentParser fill ModelArguments at 58, DatasetArguments at 418, and the stage arguments in one pass. The dispatcher that turns the name “finetuner” into a Finetuner object is deliberately boring - a name-to-class registry - but its registration block is where the extras system lives: the SGLang and vLLM inferencers join the registry only when their packages import (the availability probes are is_vllm_available at line 60 and is_sglang_available at line 64 of lmflow/utils/versioning.py), the DPO aligners require TRL, and the RAFT aligner is registered only below transformers 4.35, matching the vendored trainer it depends on. The same pattern drives the model side: AutoModel.get_model at line 12 of auto_model.py reads arch_type and returns HFDecoderModel or HFTextRegressionModel, nothing else.

The model layer is a study in mixin composition. HFModelMixin at line 43 of lmflow/models/hf_model_mixin.py runs a chain of private preparers - __prepare_tokenizer at 94, __prepare_dtype at 133, __prepare_model_config at 159, __prepare_quant_config at 203 for the QLoRA paths, __prepare_peft_config at 248, then __prepare_model_for_training at 323 or __prepare_model_for_inference at 386 depending on the phase - and exposes activate_model_for_inference at 518 and deactivate_model_for_inference at 556 so stages can borrow the model between rounds. HFDecoderModel at line 57 of lmflow/models/hf_decoder_model.py adds the tokenizer-adjacent work: tokenize at 81, encode at 234, decode at 271, inference at 313 with __vllm_inference at 430 and __sglang_inference at 456 as dedicated backend branches, prepare_inputs_for_inference at 481, and checkpoint utilities merge_lora_weights at 577 and get_peft_without_qlora at 590. The regression sibling at line 45 of lmflow/models/hf_text_regression_model.py is the 424-line reward-model class, and the multimodal path pairs CustomAutoVision2SeqModel at line 31 of lmflow/models/vision2seq_model.py with a 294-line CLIP wrapper in lmflow/models/vision_encoder/clip_encoder.py.

Data flows through one container class. Dataset at line 53 of lmflow/datasets/dataset.py wraps a Hugging Face or JSON backend behind from_dict at 150, create_from_dict at 235, map at 309, sample at 397, and train_test_split at 427, with sanity_check at 483 catching malformed instances before they reach the trainer; the multimodal sibling in lmflow/datasets/multi_modal_dataset.py adds 291 lines for image-text corpora. Tokenization lives in lmflow/tokenization/hf_decoder_model.py - blocking at 19, tokenize_function at 57, and conversation_tokenize_function at 111, which consults the template layer. That layer, lmflow/utils/conversation_template/base.py, models a chat format as TemplateComponent lists (line 18) built by formatters (StringFormatter at 115), with ConversationTemplate at 154 providing encode_conversation at 180 and post_process_pairs at 299, and ConversationTemplateForTool at 403 adding _handle_tools at 542 for function-calling formats. Thirteen per-family modules subclass it - qwen.py at 414 lines, deepseek.py at 244, llama.py with Llama2ConversationTemplate at line 16 - and the Finetuner consumes the result through group_text at line 131 of finetuner.py, which packs tokenized sequences to model_max_length exactly the way axolotl’s packing and ms-swift’s padding-free batches do.

The alignment family is where the research lives. Finetuner at line 40 (its tune method at 222) handles full, LoRA, and QLoRA runs, and LISA plugs in as DynamicLayerActivationCallback at line 8 of lisa_trainer.py: freeze_all_layers at 43, on_step_begin at 49, and switch_active_layers at 54 rotate a budget of active layers on an interval - the layerwise importance sampling from the group’s own paper, and a cousin of the memory tricks in deepspeed and colossalai. DPOAligner at line 72 of dpo_aligner.py pairs a policy and reference through TRL, while DPOv2Aligner at line 30 of dpov2_aligner.py goes deeper: convert_to_paired_dataset at 143, _calc_reward_with_length_penalty at 198, and sampling_paired_idx_from_rewards at 210 build chosen/rejected pairs by reward, with MemorySafeDPOv2Aligner at 273 wrapping the same logic in a subprocess. IterativeDPOAligner at line 29 of iterative_dpo_aligner.py orchestrates rounds - _align_single_iteration at 66 calls _do_target_model_inference at 120, then _do_reward_model_inference at 185, then _do_single_dpo_align at 210, passing DataProto batches between steps. RaftAligner at line 34 of raft_aligner.py takes the other road: _get_batch_dataset_top at 257 ranks samples by reward-model score, keeps the top fraction, and simply fine-tunes on winners via align at 545 - no preference pairs at all - which is why it carries the vendored RaftTrainer at line 209 of raft_trainer.py, 3786 lines with train at 1517 and its own get_optimizer_cls_and_kwargs at 1059. The reward models themselves are trained and served by RewardModelTuner at line 16 of rm_tuner.py and RewardModelInferencer at line 41, both sitting on the regression model class.

Serving and evaluation close the loop. Inferencer at line 45 (with create_dataloader at 99, inference at 128, and streaming at 270) is the HF-backend default; SpeculativeInferencer at 318 implements draft-then-verify decoding with autoregressive_sampling at 422; ToolInferencer at 565 answers with tool calls and executes Python via code_exec at 628. VLLMInferencer at line 37 of vllm_inferencer.py adds batch throughput with _parse_args_to_sampling_params at 51 and a memory-safe subprocess variant at 122, returning results as DataProto at line 257 of lmflow/utils/protocol.py - a tensor-dict container whose chunk at 762, concat at 815, repeat at 869, and sample_level_repeat at 952 make it a smaller cousin of the data movement in OpenRLHF’s experience buffers. Evaluator at line 46 of evaluator.py finishes the story with evaluate at 142 dispatching to _evaluate_acc_with_accelerate at 179, _evaluate_acc_with_deepspeed at 287, _evaluate_ppl at 391, and _evaluate_nll at 440, using answer_extraction at line 155 of lmflow/utils/data_utils.py to grade free-form outputs.

From Install to a Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s recommended setup targets Linux and pins version 1.0.0 or later:

git clone -b v1.0.0 https://github.com/OptimalScale/LMFlow.git
cd LMFlow
conda create -n lmflow python=3.9 -y
conda activate lmflow
conda install mpi4py
pip install -e .

Then a LoRA run on Llama-2-7B with a conversation template:

cd data && ./download.sh alpaca && cd -
bash ./scripts/run_finetune_with_lora.sh \
  --model_name_or_path meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf \
  --dataset_path data/alpaca/train_conversation \
  --conversation_template llama2 \
  --output_model_path output_models/finetuned_llama2_7b_lora

Swap the script for run_finetune_with_lisa.sh and add –lisa_activated_layers 1 –lisa_interval_steps 20 to train with LISA’s rotating layer budget, or run_finetune_with_custom_optim.sh to pick any of the 22 optimizers. The Python API is the five-call sequence from examples/finetune.py - argument classes, dispatcher, Dataset, AutoModel, tune - and extras like pip install -e ".[vllm,trl]" unlock the vLLM-backed iterative DPO loop.

Honest limits: the README states the package is fully tested on Ubuntu and only partially elsewhere; the RAFT aligner is pinned to transformers below 4.35 because of its vendored trainer; vLLM and SGLang must live in separate environments due to CUDA conflicts; and WandB reporting is on by default until you pass –report_to none. The abstraction seams are visible, though - every algorithm is one aligner class you can read top to bottom, which is rarer than it should be.
entry.summary: A source tour of LMFlow: dataclass arguments, model mixins, DPO, DPOv2, RAFT and iterative-DPO aligners, LISA layer freezing, a 22-optimizer zoo, and speculative decoding.

entry.title: One Framework from Tuning to Deployment - Inside modelscope/ms-swift

link.title: One Framework from Tuning to Deployment - Inside modelscope/ms-swift

entry.content:
ModelScope’s ms-swift has a scope that makes most fine-tuning frameworks look modest: supervised tuning, preference optimization, GRPO-style reinforcement learning, knowledge distillation, multimodal training, Megatron-backed large runs, quantized export, and deployment, all in one package. The current development line, version 4.7.0.dev0 under an Apache-2.0 license, organizes that breadth with an unusual pattern - rather than one monolithic trainer, a factory composes small mixin classes into exactly the trainer a task needs, and the same composition style repeats in the adapter system, the template engine, and the inference layer. The result is a codebase where the fastest way to understand any feature is to find its mixin.

It is also one of the few frameworks where the ModelScale ecosystem assumptions pay off visibly: datasets load straight from the Hub, templates read metadata registered alongside the models, and the CLI treats training, rollout sampling, evaluation, and deployment as sibling subcommands of one binary. For anyone who has outgrown single-purpose scripts, this is a case study in layering without sprawl. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI parses argument trees and dispatches to a trainer factory; mixins compose into SFT and RLHF trainers; templates and datasets feed training while adapters reshape models and inference engines close the loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • swift/cli/main.py is the 106-line router: parse_yaml_args at line 38 merges YAML config files with command-line flags, and cli_main at line 86 maps subcommands to entry modules.
  • swift/arguments/sft_args.py holds the 434-line SFT argument tree; the RLHF counterpart in swift/arguments/rlhf_args.py runs 773 lines.
  • swift/trainers/trainer_factory.py defines TrainerFactory at line 12, the class-composition switch for every training stage.
  • swift/trainers/mixin.py is the shared behavior core, SwiftMixin at line 70 of 1495 lines with DataLoaderMixin at line 1352.
  • swift/rlhf_trainers/grpo_trainer.py is the largest single file in the package: GRPOTrainer at line 84 of 2623 lines.
  • swift/template/base.py defines Template at line 43, the 2502-line encoder that turns conversations into tensors.
  • swift/tuners/base.py exposes SwiftModel at line 31 and the Swift facade at line 702 for ten adapter types.
  • swift/infer_engine/vllm_engine.py wraps vLLM in VllmEngine at line 121 of 968 lines.

Why You Need This

The mixin-composition pattern is the main draw. Instead of inheriting a fixed hierarchy, TrainerFactory at line 12 of trainer_factory.py picks a TRL or HF trainer class, mixes in SwiftMixin for dataset handling, adapter mounting, and loss scaling, and hands back a trainer whose behavior is assembled from parts. If you have ever wished the Hugging Face Trainer were easier to customize, or wondered how TRL-style trainers get extended without forking them, this file is a clean answer - and it contrasts nicely with the config-driven dispatch of LLaMA-Factory and the patch-first strategy of unsloth.

The template engine is the second reason. Multimodal chat models need text, images, videos, and audio interleaved into one token sequence with loss masks, and ms-swift’s Template class at line 43 of template/base.py does that encoding generically - 2502 lines covering grounding boxes, tool calls, thinking modes, and per-model quirks through a metadata system. Combined with the dataset layer’s media handling, it is one of the most complete public implementations of what “apply_chat_template” actually has to do for real model families. The RLHF stack rides on it: GRPO with async vLLM rollouts, DPO and its CPO/ORPO/KTO relatives, PPO, and Generative Knowledge Distillation all share the same data plumbing, an approach you can compare directly with OpenRLHF’s single-controller design or axolotl’s GRPO trainers.

Finally, the adapter zoo is worth the visit on its own. SwiftModel at line 31 of tuners/base.py wraps any model so that LoRA, LLaMA-Pro’s layer expansion, Restuning’s bottleneck adapters, ReFT representation edits, NEFTune noise, and more attach through one interface - a broader catalog than peft alone ships, built on top of it where possible. The Megatron subpackage extends the same argument surface to very large models the way deepspeed or colossalai users would expect, and the inference engines - vLLM, LMDeploy, SGLang, plain PyTorch - all speak one protocol module, which makes the train-to-deploy loop of lm-evaluation-harness-style benchmarking trivial to attach.

Detailed view: CLI routing, argument families, the training core with its mixin, the RLHF trainer family with rollout machinery, templates and datasets, adapters, inference engines, and the model registry.

A run begins in cli/main.py, where cli_main at line 86 resolves the subcommand - the individual entries are tiny, with cli/sft.py at 20 lines and cli/rlhf.py at 7 - and torchrun relaunching is handled by use_torchrun at line 30. Arguments layer into families: SFTArgs in arguments/sft_args.py embeds the tuner arguments of arguments/tuner_args.py, while the RLHF tree in arguments/rlhf_args.py adds rollout, reward, and vLLM server sections. Everything lands in TrainerFactory at line 12 of trainers/trainer_factory.py, a 75-line file that decides which composed trainer class to build from the stage, train type, and backend flags.

The mixin is where the real work hides. SwiftMixin at line 70 of trainers/mixin.py owns the shared lifecycle - loading model and template, mounting adapters, preparing losses - while DataLoaderMixin at line 1352 builds the batch streams, including the packing path from dataset/packing.py. Trainer construction goes through trainers/trainer.py, whose 74 lines define the SFT and CPT trainer classes on top of the mixin, and upstream Trainer behavior is adjusted by trainers/patcher.py plus the helpers in trainers/utils.py. Dataset loading flows through dataset/loader.py, a 421-line loader that mixes registered datasets with per-dataset sampling weights, backed by the registry in dataset/register.py and metadata in dataset_meta.py. The terse dataset strings the CLI accepts are parsed by DatasetSyntax at line 56 of dataset/dataset_syntax.py, whose docstring spells out the grammar - hf/ms::dataset_id or path:subset1/subset2#sample_count - so the #500 suffix in the quickstart below literally means “take 500 rows of this corpus”. The registry side is two functions: register_dataset at line 24 of dataset/register.py files DatasetMeta records declared in dataset/dataset_meta.py (DatasetMeta at line 174, SubsetDataset at line 27), and get_dataset_list at line 14 resolves names to metadata - the same three-part registry-plus-syntax pattern that templates and models use.

The RLHF family shows the same composition at its most elaborate. GRPOTrainer at line 84 of rlhf_trainers/grpo_trainer.py - 2623 lines, the package’s biggest file - composes RolloutTrainerMixin, SwiftMixin, and TRL’s GRPO trainer. RolloutTrainerMixin at line 91 of rlhf_trainers/rollout_mixin.py is the 1853-line bridge between training and generation: AsyncGenerateCallback at line 66 overlaps sampling with optimization, SyncRefModelCallback at line 78 keeps a remote reference model fresh, and the mixin drives either an in-process vLLM engine or the external server client at rlhf_trainers/vllm_client.py, 550 lines that manage weight sync and cache reset over HTTP. The preference branch centers on rlhf_trainers/dpo_trainer.py at 519 lines (with CPO and ORPO variants nearby), PPO at rlhf_trainers/ppo_trainer.py, KTO at 130 lines, reward-model training in reward_trainer.py, and the distillation pair of gkd_trainer.py and gkd_loss.py - Generative Knowledge Distillation where the student learns from the teacher’s own generations.

Templates deserve their own paragraph because they carry the multimodal weight. TemplateMeta in template/template_meta.py declares a model family’s system prompt, stop words, and special tokens; register_template at line 16 of template/register.py files hundreds of these registrations, and get_template at line 55 resolves one from model metadata read out of the checkpoint directory. The base Template at line 43 of template/base.py then encodes messages - including vision and audio inputs through template/vision_utils.py - into input ids, labels, and loss masks that the trainers consume directly. The adapter side mirrors this registry style: SwiftModel at line 31 and Swift at line 702 of tuners/base.py activate LoRA from tuners/lora.py with its custom tuners/lora_layers.py, LLaMA-Pro block expansion from tuners/llamapro.py, and the rest from sibling modules.

Serving and the model registry close the loop. InferEngine at line 22 of infer_engine/infer_engine.py defines the common request surface; VllmEngine at line 121 of infer_engine/vllm_engine.py implements it for vLLM (with compatibility patches like _patch_vllm_dp_coordinator_timeout at line 54), while transformers_engine.py, lmdeploy_engine.py, and sglang_engine.py cover the other backends, all speaking the request shapes in infer_engine/protocol.py. Under everything sits the model registry: model_arch.py at 926 lines maps architectures to module names, register.py at 689 lines files per-model metadata and loading adjustments, and patcher.py at 726 lines carries the per-family fixes. Model names themselves live as enum members in model/constant.py, 313 lines where LLMModelType at line 6, MLLMModelType at line 144, and reward-model and BERT entries at lines 130 and 136 merge into a ModelType union at line 295 - the same three-part pattern the template and dataset systems use, which is the codebase’s real signature.

From Install to a Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s 13GB one-GPU run:

pip install ms-swift
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 swift sft \
    --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 \
    --tuner_type lora \
    --dataset AI-ModelScope/alpaca-gpt4-data-zh#500 \
              AI-ModelScope/alpaca-gpt4-data-en#500 \
    --lora_rank 8 --lora_alpha 32 \
    --target_modules all-linear \
    --max_length 2048 --output_dir output

Inference and export use the same style:

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 swift infer --adapters output/checkpoint-xx --infer_backend vllm
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 swift export --adapters output/checkpoint-xx --merge_lora true

The Python API mirrors it: swift.llm exposes the same argument objects, so a script can construct TrainArguments and call the trainer factory directly.

Honest limits: the argument surface is huge and moves fast between minor versions, so blog posts and tutorials age quickly; Megatron and RLHF paths assume multi-GPU comfort; and the mixin composition, while elegant, means a debugger steps through more classes than a monolithic trainer would. The payoff is breadth with visible seams - almost everything is one registry entry away from view.
entry.summary: A source tour of ms-swift: a TrainerFactory that composes mixins into trainers, a 2500-line Template engine for chat and multimodal encoding, ten adapter types behind SwiftModel, RLHF trainers with vLLM rollouts, and inference engines that share one protocol.

entry.title: Ray, vLLM, and One Controller - Inside OpenRLHF/OpenRLHF

link.title: Ray, vLLM, and One Controller - Inside OpenRLHF/OpenRLHF

entry.content:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback is the most distributed-shaped problem in LLM training: you need a policy being trained, a reference model frozen in time, a reward model scoring outputs, a critic estimating values, and a generation engine producing rollouts - each with different resource needs, all cooperating every step. OpenRLHF, the framework behind the REINFORCE++ line of work and a teaching case in CMU’s graduate NLP course, answers with a single-controller architecture: one Python process holds the training logic while Ray actors hold the models, and a fleet of vLLM engines does nothing but generate. Release 0.11.3 under an Apache-2.0 license fits all of this into a remarkably small codebase, which is exactly why it rewards a careful read.

The whole system speaks one data language. A dataclass called Experience - prompts, responses, log probabilities, rewards, values, losses - flows from the rollout engines through a replay buffer into the trainers, and every algorithm from PPO to GRPO to RLOO is a different way of filling its fields and weighting its updates. If you want to understand how production RLHF systems actually share state across heterogeneous model workers, this is the clearest public map available. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: CLI entries feed the trainers; models and losses form the mathematical core; Ray actors and vLLM engines carry the distributed execution while a DeepSpeed strategy manages sharding.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • openrlhf/cli/train_ppo_ray.py is the 771-line PPO entry whose train at line 19 parses the deeply nested argument tree and assembles the actor group.
  • openrlhf/datasets/prompts_dataset.py defines PromptDataset at line 48 with preprocessing at line 26 for chat templates and mixing probabilities.
  • openrlhf/models/actor.py wraps the policy in Actor at line 54 with a ZeRO-3 weight-mapping patch at line 16.
  • openrlhf/models/loss.py is the algorithm catalog: PolicyLoss at line 116, ValueLoss at line 262, PairWiseLoss at line 301, DPOLoss at line 329.
  • openrlhf/trainer/ppo_trainer.py holds BasePPOTrainer at line 148 and PPOTrainer at line 450 of its 599 lines.
  • openrlhf/trainer/ray/ppo_actor.py is the distributed training loop, ActorPPOTrainer at line 37 of 683 lines.
  • openrlhf/trainer/ray/vllm_engine.py defines RolloutRayActor at line 34 and the fleet factory create_vllm_engines at line 209.
  • openrlhf/utils/deepspeed/deepspeed.py implements DeepspeedStrategy at line 37, the 788-line configuration engine behind every model actor.

Why You Need This

The framework field splits into two camps: monoliths that own everything and thin wrappers that delegate everything. OpenRLHF takes a third path that is worth copying - the coordination problem is solved once, in one place, and the algorithms ride on top. Where TRL (the library unsloth patches) embeds RL into the Hugging Face Trainer, and LLaMA-Factory exposes DPO as one stage among many, OpenRLHF makes the distributed loop itself the product. Reading it clarifies what PPO actually requires at scale: synchronized weight broadcasts to inference engines, advantage estimation over batched experiences, and a KL leash to the reference model.

The weight-sync problem is the deepest lesson here. During RLHF, the policy changes every step, but the vLLM engines that generate rollouts hold their own copy of the weights. OpenRLHF solves this with explicit broadcast paths - training step finishes, weights flow to every rollout engine over NCCL, generation resumes - and the source shows the machinery without abstraction: initialization of the sync group, per-engine broadcast calls, and sleep modes that let training and inference share GPUs. Anyone who has wondered how hybrid engines work will find the answer written in plain PyTorch and Ray.

Finally, the algorithms are honest about being small. Once experiences are collected, PPO, REINFORCE++, GRPO, and RLOO differ by a few lines of advantage estimation and loss masking - the repo’s own notes explain how REINFORCE++-baseline outperformed GRPO in stability for reasoning models. That insight, that the algorithm is the easy part and the plumbing is the hard part, is the reason this codebase exists, and it pairs naturally with the evaluation tour of lm-evaluation-harness for scoring the resulting models, or with axolotl’s async GRPO trainers as a different point on the same design space. Even non-RL parts - the DeepSpeed integration, the sequence-length balancing - are useful references alongside deepspeed and colossalai.

Detailed view: CLI entries with datasets, the model and loss core, single-process trainers, the experience machinery, Ray actors and rollout engines, and infrastructure utilities.

Start where a run starts. train at line 19 of cli/train_ppo_ray.py builds a DeepspeedStrategy, loads PromptDataset from datasets/prompts_dataset.py, and creates a RayActorGroup at line 202 of trainer/ray/launcher.py - the same class that will later spawn reference, reward, and critic actors (BaseModelActor at line 54, ReferenceModelActor at line 105, RewardModelActor at line 158 of that file). The single-controller idea lives in this split: launcher.py knows how to place models on GPUs, while the trainer process knows the algorithm and calls the actors remotely.

The experience path is the heart. RemoteExperienceMaker at line 19 of trainer/ppo_utils/experience_maker.py sends prompts to the rollout engines, collects log probabilities from the policy and reference models, scores with the reward model, and packs everything into the Experience dataclass at line 29 of trainer/ppo_utils/experience.py - a 283-line module that also handles batching (make_experience_batch at line 199), padding removal at line 236, and sequence balancing at line 250. Experiences land in NaiveReplayBuffer at line 17 of trainer/ppo_utils/replay_buffer.py, and the KL leash is controlled by AdaptiveKLController at line 4 of trainer/ppo_utils/kl_controller.py - all 29 lines of it, because a controller only needs a target and an update rule.

The distributed loop then takes over in trainer/ray/ppo_actor.py. ActorPPOTrainer at line 37 initializes the vLLM sync group at line 108, runs the generation-training alternation in ppo_train at line 153, executes each gradient step in training_step at line 259, and pushes refreshed weights to every rollout engine through broadcast_to_vllm at line 409. The concrete worker, PolicyModelActor at line 494, wraps the Actor model with state offloading - offload_states at line 658 lets the policy sleep while another model uses its GPUs - and trainer/ray/vllm_engine.py mirrors the other side: RolloutRayActor at line 34 hosts a vLLM engine per Ray process, while create_vllm_engines at line 209 sizes the fleet from tensor-parallel and engine-count flags. The single-process cousin, PPOTrainer at line 450 of trainer/ppo_trainer.py after BasePPOTrainer at line 148, shares the same experience machinery for colocated setups, and the async variant in trainer/ppo_trainer_async.py overlaps generation with training.

Small helpers round out the loop with the same economy. prepare_datasets at line 26 of trainer/ppo_trainer.py splits train and evaluation prompt sources, compute_eval_metrics at line 82 runs evaluation rollouts between training phases, batch_vllm_engine_call at line 314 of trainer/ray/vllm_engine.py fans a method call out across the engine fleet while keeping only rank zero’s return value, and aggregate_loss at line 11 of models/loss.py merges policy, value, and KL terms into one weighted objective so a training step is a single backward call.

The math lives in two files. models/loss.py is the full algorithm catalog in 364 lines: SFTLoss at line 87 for supervised runs, PolicyLoss at line 116 implementing the PPO-clip objective with optional dual clipping, ValueLoss at line 262 for the critic, PairWiseLoss at line 301 and LogExpLoss at line 316 for reward modeling, and DPOLoss at line 329 for direct preference optimization. models/model.py builds the value-headed siblings of any causal LM through get_llm_for_sequence_regression at line 21, with the reward variant at _get_reward_model line 177 and the critic at _get_critic_model line 245 - the trick that lets any pretrained checkpoint become a reward model by appending a score head. The Actor wrapper at line 54 of models/actor.py handles generation-mode switching and packing-aware forward passes, with ring-attention support from models/ring_attn_utils.py for long contexts.

Around the core sit the supporting trainers and utilities. trainer/sft_trainer.py (SFTTrainer at line 13), trainer/dpo_trainer.py (DPOTrainer at line 12), and trainer/rm_trainer.py (RewardModelTrainer at line 12) cover the pre-RL stages of the alignment recipe, each with a matching CLI in cli/ and dataset in datasets/ - reward_dataset.py holds the chosen/rejected loader for RM training. Agent-based reinforcement learning gets utils/agent.py: AgentExecutorBase at line 13, MultiTurnAgentExecutor at line 32, and SingleTurnAgentExecutor at line 188 turn arbitrary reward functions into rollout sources, which is how the repo trains on verifiable math and code rewards. Infrastructure details that quietly decide performance get their own files too - DeepspeedStrategy at line 37 of utils/deepspeed/deepspeed.py owns ZeRO stages, packing, and sleep modes, while karmarkar_karp at line 24 of utils/seqlen_balancing.py partitions variable-length sequences across micro-batches so one 4k-token sample cannot stall a whole step.

From Install to an Aligned Model

The README’s recommended path runs in Docker with vLLM:

pip install openrlhf[vllm]
ray start --head --node-ip-address 0.0.0.0 --num-gpus 8

Then submit a PPO run with hybrid engine settings:

ray job submit --address="http://127.0.0.1:8265" \
  -- python3 -m openrlhf.cli.train_ppo_ray \
  --ref.num_nodes 1 --ref.num_gpus_per_node 8 \
  --actor.model_name_or_path OpenRLHF/Llama-3-8b-sft-mixture \
  --reward.model_name_or_path OpenRLHF/Llama-3-8b-rm-700k \
  --vllm.num_engines 4 --vllm.tensor_parallel_size 2 \
  --train.batch_size 128 --rollout.batch_size 1024 \
  --zero.stage 3 --adam.offload True

Algorithm variants are single flags: --algo.advantage.estimator group_norm becomes GRPO, reinforce becomes REINFORCE++, rloo becomes RLOO.

Honest limits: the framework assumes you can afford a Ray cluster and knows it - the README recommends Docker and multi-GPU nodes; vLLM version pinning matters because the weight-sync path touches engine internals; and the argument surface is enormous, since every strategy knob is a CLI flag. What you get in exchange is a complete, readable map of distributed RLHF that fits in an afternoon.
entry.summary: A source tour of OpenRLHF: a single-controller design over Ray actors, vLLM rollout engines kept in sync with the policy, an Experience dataclass flowing between generation and training, REINFORCE++ and GRPO losses, and DeepSpeed-backed model actors.

entry.title: The 52K Recipe That Started a Thousand Fine-Tunes - Inside tatsu-lab/stanford_alpaca

link.title: The 52K Recipe That Started a Thousand Fine-Tunes - Inside tatsu-lab/stanford_alpaca

entry.content:
Some repositories matter because of their engineering, and some because of what they proved. stanford_alpaca, from five Stanford grad students advised by Tatsunori Hashimoto, is the second kind: fourteen files that showed a 7B LLaMA model fine-tuned on 52K machine-generated instruction examples could behave similarly to text-davinci-003 on the Self-Instruct evaluation suite. The whole data generation cost less than $500, the fine-tuning script is 222 lines, and the release pattern - code under Apache 2.0, data and weight diffs under CC BY NC 4.0 - became the template an entire ecosystem copied. Every toolbox we have toured in this series, from LLaMA-Factory to axolotl to ms-swift, descends from the recipe in this folder.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: seed tasks and the generation template feed the self-instruct loop, whose API client writes the 52K dataset; the fine-tuning script consumes it with FSDP or DeepSpeed, and the weight-diff tool closes the release loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • generate_instruction.py is the 217-line generation loop: encode_prompt at line 27, post_process_gpt3_response at 44, and generate_instruction_following_data at 110, with a rouge-L similarity threshold of 0.7 at line 196.
  • prompt.txt is the generation template - seven numbered requirements asking for 20 diverse task instructions per completion, including the famous accidental duplicate numbering the authors flag for future users.
  • seed_tasks.jsonl holds 175 human-written seeds, from seed_task_0’s breakfast suggestion onward, each with an instruction and one instance.
  • utils.py is the API client: OpenAIDecodingArguments at line 25, openai_completion at 39 with retry-and-shrink backoff at lines 116-120, and the jdump/jload JSON helpers at 148 and 168.
  • alpaca_data.json is the artifact itself: 52,002 entries with instruction, input, and output fields, 20,679 of them carrying a non-empty input.
  • train.py is the entire fine-tuning story in 222 lines: PROMPT_DICT at 31, smart_tokenizer_and_embedding_resize at 65, preprocess at 112, SupervisedDataset at 127, DataCollatorForSupervisedDataset at 157, and train at 182.
  • configs/default_offload_opt_param.json is the DeepSpeed escape hatch - ZeRO stage 3 with CPU offload for both optimizer states and parameters.
  • weight_diff.py is the release mechanism: make_diff at line 25, recover at 71, and a naive-but-effective integrity check at 129 that asserts a checkpoint-wide sum of 50637.1836.

Why You Need This

Read this repo to see how little a landmark result takes. There is no framework here, no plugin registry, no YAML - just four Python files and one JSON dataset. Where LLaMA-Factory routes dozens of model families through a template registry and OpenRLHF distributes a PPO controller over Ray, Alpaca formats 52K strings with two templates, masks the prompt tokens, and hands everything to the stock Hugging Face Trainer. The hyperparameters in the README - global batch 128, learning rate 2e-5 for 7B and 1e-5 for 13B, three epochs, max length 512 - fit in a five-row table that a thousand follow-up papers then cited or tweaked.

The data generation half is the more interesting source lesson: it is Self-Instruct with batch decoding. Instead of one instruction per API call, encode_prompt at line 27 stuffs three sampled seed examples into a template that requests twenty at once, cutting cost by an order of magnitude, and post_process_gpt3_response at line 44 parses all twenty back out with a regex. The filtering gauntlet in between - length limits, a keyword blacklist, and rouge-L deduplication against everything generated so far - is a compact masterclass in keeping a synthetic dataset diverse, and it directly prefigures the synthetic-data machinery inside later toolboxes like ms-swift.

Finally, the weight-diff mechanism is a period piece worth understanding: in March 2023 the LLaMA license forbade redistributing weights, so the repo published only the difference between Alpaca-7B and LLaMA-7B, recoverable in minutes by anyone with the base checkpoint. weight_diff.py makes the whole chain auditable - subtract raw from tuned, add raw back, verify with a checksum - and the licensing split (Apache code, CC BY NC data, CC BY NC diffs) is spelled out in three separate license files. The constraint is gone now, but the pattern of shipping provable artifacts rather than promises shaped how peft adapters, LoRA deltas, and model diffs get shared to this day.

Detailed view: the self-instruct loop from template to filters, the batched API client with backoff, the dataset, every stage of the 222-line fine-tuning script, the sharding recipes, and the weight-diff tooling.

The generation loop rewards close reading. generate_instruction_following_data at line 110 of generate_instruction.py loads the 175 seed tasks at line 121, resumes from regen.json if one exists at line 132, and then loops: sample three seeds at line 156, encode them via encode_prompt at 27 - which appends a numbered “21. Instruction:” cue after the examples - and fire request_batch_size prompts at the completions endpoint through utils.openai_completion at line 167 with max_tokens hard-coded to 3072 at line 162 and stop sequences tuned to catch the twentieth item. post_process_gpt3_response at line 44 splits the response on “###” markers, discards a truncated final item when the finish reason is “length” at line 52, and runs the gauntlet: instructions must be 4 to 150 words at line 64, must avoid the eighteen-word blacklist spanning lines 67-86 (image, graph, draw, plot, video, and friends - tasks a text model cannot do), must not start with “Write a program” at line 94, punctuation at 97, or a non-ASCII character at 100. Survivors then face the dedup gate: rouge-L F-measure against every prior instruction, computed in a multiprocessing pool at line 187, with anything scoring above 0.7 dropped at line 196. Each keeper is stored with its ten most similar neighbors and an average similarity score at lines 193-201, which is how the dataset release ships its own diversity audit.

The API client in utils.py is a period-accurate artifact of the old completions API. OpenAIDecodingArguments at line 25 dataclasses the sampling knobs; openai_completion at line 39 batches prompts at line 87, tags each choice with total token usage at line 110, and - the part still worth copying - handles failures with two distinct branches at lines 113-120: context-length errors shrink max_tokens by twenty percent and retry, everything else sleeps and retries. The logit_bias trick at line 172 of generate_instruction.py, suppressing the end-of-text token so all twenty tasks arrive in one response, shows how much behavior you can steer without touching the model.

The training half of train.py is deliberately minimal but gets the details right. PROMPT_DICT at line 31 defines the two prompt templates the README quotes; SupervisedDataset at line 127 formats every example, appends the EOS token to each target at line 141, and tokenizes everything up front through preprocess at line 112, which tokenizes concatenated source-plus-target and blanks out the prompt span with IGNORE_INDEX = -100 at line 123 so the loss is computed on responses only. DataCollatorForSupervisedDataset at line 157 right-pads input_ids with the pad token and labels with -100 at lines 164-167, matching the README’s note that sequences are right-padded. The most reused function in the file is smart_tokenizer_and_embedding_resize at line 65: when the LLaMA tokenizer lacks pad, bos, or unk tokens, train at line 182 adds them, resizes the embedding matrices, and mean-initializes the new rows from existing embeddings at lines 81-85 - the fix every early LLaMA fine-tune needed, imported by weight_diff.py at its line 21 so the diff math lines up token-for-token.

Distribution is left to recipes rather than code. The README’s primary command runs torchrun with FSDP full_shard auto_wrap, wrapping LlamaDecoderLayer on four A100 80G GPUs, with an OPT-6.7B variant swapping in OPTDecoderLayer - and the OOM section does the arithmetic a newcomer needs: 7B parameters times four bytes times four roles is roughly 112GB naive, parameter sharding removes the redundant copies, and CPU offload via the ZeRO-3 config in configs/default_offload_opt_param.json trades runtime for headroom, with LoRA mentioned as the path to about 28GB. Those three rungs - full fine-tune, offload, adapter - are exactly the ladder deepspeed, accelerate, and peft industrialized, and modern toolboxes like unsloth and axolotl still expose the same choices behind friendlier flags.

The weight-diff file closes the loop with unusual transparency. make_diff at line 25 of weight_diff.py loads both checkpoints in float32 on one device, subtracts in place with add_ at line 64, and saves the result; recover at line 71 loads the raw LLaMA checkpoint plus the diff, adds it back at line 125, and runs a self-described naive integrity check at line 129 - summing every recovered tensor and asserting the total is 50637.1836 within 1e-2 - before optionally generating a 100-token answer to a built-in instruction at lines 138-148 as a smoke test. The dataset itself is documented in datasheet.md and model_card.md, and the training data’s non-commercial license is why the authors kept the live demo rather than the weights. For evaluating instruction-following descendants of this recipe, the natural companion is our tour of lm-evaluation-harness; for what came after preference tuning replaced pure SFT, see openrlhf and lmflow.

From Install to a Fine-Tuned Model

Reproducing the 7B run takes one install and one torchrun command:

pip install -r requirements.txt
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 --master_port=<your_random_port> train.py \
    --model_name_or_path <your_path_to_hf_converted_llama_ckpt_and_tokenizer> \
    --data_path ./alpaca_data.json \
    --bf16 True \
    --output_dir <your_output_dir> \
    --num_train_epochs 3 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 8 \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --lr_scheduler_type "cosine" \
    --fsdp "full_shard auto_wrap" \
    --fsdp_transformer_layer_cls_to_wrap 'LlamaDecoderLayer' \
    --tf32 True

Data generation and weight recovery are one-liners with fire:
